newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Polls open for Serbia's run-off municipal vote.
newsitem.headline: Polls open for Serbia's run-off municipal vote.

text.p: Serbia held a run-off election on Sunday for municipal councils two weeks after President Slobodan Milosevic's leftist coalition scored a resounding victory in national polls.
The opposition coalition hoped to make up for a poor result in the federal election on November 3 with a strong showing in the capital Belgrade and other major towns.
In the first round of local elections, only about 2,000 city council members managed to win a majority out of a total of 7,670 races.
A few hours hours after polling stations opened at 7 a.m., the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition issued a statement alleging abuses in Belgrade and several other districts.
The Zajedno coalition charged that the authorities prevented opposition members from taking part in some electoral boards, which supervise ballot counting and voting procedures.

In five polling stations around the central town of Lazarevac, police threw out Zajedno and nationalist Radical party members from the electoral boards and threatened to arrest them if they returned, the opposition statement said.

Three ruling coalition candidates in Smederervska Palanka were also serving as members of the electoral boards, according to the opposition, and were allegedly asking voters, "Did you come to vote for us or those traitors?"
The opposition accused Serbian authorities in the southern town of Nis of hiring body guards to prevent Zajedno members from joining the work of the electoral board.
The body guards were allegedly linked to the notorious paramilitary commander Zeljko Raznatovic, known as "Arkan", the statement said.
There was no immediate response to the allegations from Serbian authorities.

Even if the opposition coalition manages to win control of some city councils, political analysts say real power will remain at the national level with Milosevic -- who retains tight control over the police, the state-run media and the economy.
Milosevic's coalition won a big parliamentary majority in the federal polls held two weeks ago in the remaining Yugoslav republics of Serbia and Montenegro.
The coalition is comprised of the ruling Socialist party, New Democracy and the Yugoslav United Left, led by Milosevic's powerful wife, Mirjana Markovic.
